links.note: 831 defines folly as taking up what harms and letting gain go (ஏதங்கொண்டு ஊதியம் போக விடல்). 422 defines understanding as the reverse movement: turning away from evil and steering toward good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது). Read together, the two definitions are mirror images, so folly in 831 is not a lack of information but the wrong choice between two things in view.

831 says folly is to let gain go (ஊதியம் போக விடல்). 797 uses the same two words to say what gain is: giving up and leaving the friendship of fools (ஊதியம் என்பது ... பேதையார் கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்). The fool lets gain go, and for everyone else letting the fool go is the gain.

831 says folly is accepting harm and letting gain go. 925 gives a concrete case in drinking: handing over wealth to receive ignorance of one's own body (பொருள்கொடுத்து மெய்யறியாமை கொளல்), which it traces to கையறியாமை, not knowing what to do. The drinker's purchase is 831's exchange carried out literally.

832 calls it the folly of follies to set one's love on what is not for one's hand (காதன்மை கையல்லதன்கட் செயல்); Parimelazhagar takes கையல்லது as forbidden conduct, Manakkudavar as a thing one cannot get. 141 calls the desire for a woman who is another's possession a folly (பிறன்பொருளாள் பெட்டொழுகும் பேதைமை). 141 is a case that fits both readings of 832: what is desired there is both forbidden and not one's own.

832 names as the worst folly a liking (காதன்மை) for what is not fit for one. 439 gives the matching instruction: do not set your desire on a deed that yields no good (நயவற்க நன்றி பயவா வினை). Both locate the error in the wanting, before any deed is done.

833 lists four absences as the fool's work: no shame, no inquiry, no tenderness, no care for anything (நாணாமை நாடாமை நாரின்மை யாதொன்றும் பேணாமை பேதை தொழில்). 428 defines folly as not fearing what should be feared and calls fearing it the work of the knowing (அறிவார் தொழில்). Both define folly as a missing response where one is due, and both set it out as a characteristic தொழில்.

833 puts shamelessness (நாணாமை) first among the fool's traits. 1018 says what that trait costs: if one is not ashamed of what makes others ashamed, the fault is one that virtue itself would be ashamed of (அறம் நாணத் தக்கது உடைத்து); Parimelazhagar reads it as virtue leaving him. 1018 supplies the consequence that 833 leaves unstated.

833 describes the fool by four negations. 865 describes the ideal enemy to have by a similar string: he does not look to the way, does not do what is fitting, does not look to blame, has no character (வழிநோக்கான் ... பழிநோக்கான் பண்பிலன்), and so is sweet to his foes. The same profile that 833 treats as a moral portrait is, in the chapter on enmity, a strategic weakness.

391 commands two things: learn flawlessly, and having learned, stand in keeping with it (கற்றபின் நிற்க அதற்குத் தக). 834 describes the person who completes the first and even teaches it but fails the second, not restraining himself (தானடங்கா), and says there is no greater fool. 834 is the negative case of 391's second clause.

130 praises the one who guards against anger and, having learned, is restrained (கற்றடங்கல் ஆற்றுவான்): virtue itself seeks him out. 834 names the one who has read, understood and taught but is not restrained (ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் ... தானடங்கா) the greatest of fools. Both treat learning and அடங்கல் as a pair in which the learning is judged by the restraint.

834 presents a puzzle: a person who has studied, understood and taught, and still does not restrain himself. 373 offers the chapter on fate's account of such a person: however many subtle books one studies, one's own underlying understanding prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்), which Parimelazhagar takes as the folly given by fate. 373 explains how the fool of 834 is possible.

398 says learning acquired in one birth is a protection through seven (ஒருமைக்கண் ... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). 835 uses the same one-to-seven frame for the fool: in one birth he can make the mire he will sink in through seven (ஒருமைச் செயலாற்றும் ... எழுமையும் தான்புக்கழுந்தும் அளறு). The pairing shows the frame cutting both ways: a single life's work carries forward as safety or as hell.

126 says that drawing in the five senses in one birth, like a tortoise, is a protection for seven (ஒருமையுள் ... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). 835 says the fool's doing in one birth produces a hell for seven. With 834 just before it defining the fool as one who does not restrain himself, 835 reads as the reverse of 126.

835 calls the fool's destination an அளறு, a mire or hell, into which he enters and sinks (புக்கழுந்தும்). 919 calls the shoulders of women who draw no line the அளறு in which base men sink (பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு). 919 uses for one present indulgence the image that 835 uses for the result of a whole life of folly.

836 says that when a fool who does not know the way of doing (கையறியாப் பேதை) takes up a task, the task fails (பொய்படும்) and he himself ends in fetters. 468 says effort not made by the right means will collapse (பொத்துப் படும்) even with many standing by to protect it. Parimelazhagar glosses both verbs as புரைபடும்; 468 states the rule about method and 836 adds the cost to the doer.

836 describes the fool as கையறியா, not knowing how to act. 925 uses the same compound, கையறியாமை, as the cause of paying money to lose awareness of oneself in drink. In both verses the word names a practical ignorance that ends in the person binding or losing himself.

524 says the fruit of having gained wealth is to live surrounded by one's kin (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட ஒழுகல்). 837 says that when a fool comes into great wealth, strangers eat their fill and his own people go hungry (ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர்பசிப்பர்). The fool's wealth fails exactly the purpose 524 assigns to wealth.

837 says a fool's great wealth feeds strangers (ஏதிலார்) while his own go hungry. 1009 says wealth amassed by giving up love, denying oneself and ignoring virtue will be taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). The miser and the fool arrive at the same result by opposite routes, one by holding wealth back and one by letting it go to the wrong people.

837 speaks of great wealth that has come to a fool (பெருஞ்செல்வம் உற்றக்கடை) and benefits the wrong people. 1000 says great wealth obtained by one without character (பண்பிலான் பெற்ற பெருஞ்செல்வம்) is like good milk spoiled by its vessel. Parimelazhagar notes on both verses that the verb marks wealth received and not made; both hold that the holder's defect ruins what the wealth could do.

838 says a fool getting something into his hand is like a man already deranged getting drunk (மையல் ஒருவன் களித்தற்று). 977 says that even distinction, if it falls to the unworthy, turns wholly into acts of excess (இறப்பே புரிந்த தொழிற்றாம்). Both say a good thing landing on the wrong person does not improve him but amplifies what he already is.

838 likens a fool's possession to drunkenness added to derangement. 408 says fortune lodged with the unlearned is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு). Both deny that wealth is a good independent of its holder; 838 gives the image and 408 the comparative judgment.

394 says the way of the learned is to meet so that others are glad and to part so that others think of them (உவப்பத் தலைக்கூடி உள்ளப் பிரிதல்). 839 says, with irony, that the friendship of fools is very sweet because parting brings no pain at all (பிரிவின்கண் பீழை தருவதொன்றில்). Both measure a bond by what is felt at parting; 839 states it from the empty side.

839 says parting from fools gives no pain. 782 says the friendship of fools shrinks like the moon after it is full (மதிப் பின்னீர பேதையார் நட்பு). Parimelazhagar connects the two in his note on 839: because the friendship wears away day by day, there is nothing left to hurt when it ends.

839 says there is nothing painful in parting from fools. 797 goes a step further: giving up and leaving the friendship of fools is what gain means (ஊதியம் என்பது ... பேதையார் கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்). 839 makes the parting painless and 797 makes it a profit.

840 likens a fool entering an assembly of the worthy to setting an unwashed foot on a bed (கழாஅக்கால் பள்ளியுள் வைத்தற்று). 720 likens speaking before those not of one's own kind to nectar spilled in an unclean yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து). The two are mirror images of the same mismatch: the unclean thing brought into the clean place, and the precious thing let fall in the unclean place.

840 treats the fool's mere entry (புகல்) into the company of the worthy as a defilement; Parimelazhagar adds that the assembly itself is lowered by it. 403 allows that even the unlearned are very good if they can stay silent before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 403 leaves a condition under which presence is acceptable, though its subject is the unlearned and 840's is the fool.

841 says lack of understanding is the lack among lacks, and the world does not count other lack as lack (பிறிதின்மை இன்மையா வையாது உலகு). 430 says those with understanding have everything and those without it have nothing, whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்). The chapter on understanding and the chapter on its absence state the same accounting from the two sides.

841 uses the formula இன்மையுள் இன்மை, the poverty of poverties, for lack of understanding. 153 uses the identical formula for turning away a guest (விருந்தொரால்), and then praises forbearance toward the ignorant. The same superlative is given to two different things, each of which a person can suffer from while owning goods. (The edition's text of 153 has a typo in the first word; Parimelazhagar's gloss confirms இன்மையுள்.)

841 says the world does not count lack of other things as lack; Pope and Manakkudavar take பிறிதின்மை as lack of wealth. 1041 says nothing is as painful as poverty except poverty itself (இன்மையின் இன்மையே இன்னாதது). The two conflict if 841 is read as ranking material want below ignorance in all respects; if 841 speaks only of how the world judges and 1041 of how want feels, they can stand together.

842 says that when a person without understanding gives gladly, the cause is nothing but the receiver's தவம். 70 says a son's service to his father is to make people ask what the father did as penance (என்நோற்றான் கொல்) to have him. Both use the same figure, explaining a good by the stored merit of the one who benefits; 70 uses it as praise of the son and 842 to deny the giver any credit.

92 treats giving with a glad heart (அகனமர்ந்து ஈதல்) as a real good, surpassed only by a glad face and sweet speech. 842 takes the same act, giving with a glad heart (நெஞ்சுவந்து ஈதல்), and says that in a person without understanding it reflects only the receiver's merit. 842 limits 92's valuation: the glad gift counts for the giver only when understanding is behind it, which is how Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read it.

843 says the suffering those without understanding inflict on themselves is hard even for their enemies to inflict (செறுவார்க்கும் செய்தல் அரிது). 165 says that for the envious, envy is enough: it brings ruin even when enemies fail to (ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது). Both measure an inner defect against an outside enemy and find the defect the more effective.

843 says the fool harms himself beyond what an enemy could. 434 says one's own fault is the enemy that brings ruin (குற்றமே அற்றந் தரூஉம் பகை) and is therefore the thing to guard against. 434 gives the general principle of which 843 is the case of the person who cannot do the guarding.

843 states generally that those without understanding torment themselves (தாந்தம்மைப் பீழிக்கும் பீழை). 847, in the same chapter, names one way it happens: the person without understanding lets the precious மறை slip and so does great harm to himself by himself (பெருமிறை தானே தனக்கு). 847 is a specific instance of 843's claim, with the same stress on தானே.

844 defines வெண்மை, literally whiteness, as the conceit that says 'we have ஒண்மை', brightness. 714 uses the same pair: be bright before the bright (ஒளியார்முன் ஒள்ளியர்) and take the colour of white plaster before the வெளியார், the blank. In both, white stands for emptiness of understanding and bright for its presence; 844 adds that the blank person is the one who claims the brightness.

844 locates want of understanding in the pride (செருக்கு) of saying 'we are bright'. 978 says smallness adorns itself in admiration of itself (சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து) while greatness bows. Both make self-admiration the identifying mark of the deficient state, one for understanding and one for stature.

844 says the claim to ஒண்மை is itself what வெண்மை is. 404 says that however good an unlearned person's ஒட்பம் may be, those with understanding do not accept it (கொள்ளார் அறிவுடையார்). 404 shows the other side of 844's self-assessment: the brightness one credits to oneself is not credited by those able to judge.

391 tells one to learn what is to be learned without flaw (கற்க கசடற) and then stand by it. 845 uses the same phrase for what a person has truly mastered (கசடற வல்லதூஉம்) and says that carrying on as if one knew what one has not learned (கல்லாத மேற்கொண்டொழுகல்) brings doubt even on that. Pretence undoes the standing of the very learning 391 asks for.

845 says one false claim to learning casts doubt on what one has mastered without flaw. 128 says that if even one bad word has its effect, the good comes to nothing (நன்றாகாதாகி விடும்). Both describe a single lapse spreading backward over what was sound, in knowledge and in speech.

405 says an unlearned person's standing gives way once he meets others and speaks (சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்). 845 describes a further loss for one who has some real learning: by taking on what he has not learned, he puts even his genuine mastery in doubt (ஐயம் தரும்). 405 is the exposure of a claim; 845 is the damage the exposure does to what was true.

846 asks whether covering one's nakedness is not itself small-minded when one's faults are left uncovered (தம்வயின் குற்றம் மறையா வழி); Parimelazhagar takes covering faults to mean removing them. 278 speaks of many who, with stain in the mind, bathe and go about concealed (மனத்தது மாசாக ... நீராடி மறைந்தொழுகு). Both set a bodily propriety, clothing or bathing, against an inner fault it does nothing about.

846 pairs அற்றம் and குற்றம் with the verb மறை: the petty cover their nakedness and leave their own faults uncovered. 980 uses the same three words of how one treats others: greatness covers another's அற்றம், smallness speaks only of faults (அற்றம் மறைக்கும் பெருமை ... குற்றமே கூறிவிடும்). Read together, covering is owed to others' exposure and to one's own faults, and the small person fails at both.

846 treats clothing the body as trivial beside dealing with one's faults. 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for any living being, and the distinction of humans is having shame (ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல நாணுடைமை மாந்தர் சிறப்பு). 1012 gives the reason behind 846: dress is common to all, and what marks a person is shame at fault.

847 says a person without understanding lets the precious மறை slip (அருமறை சோரும்) and so harms himself. Manakkudavar takes மறை as a secret let out to others, a reading Parimelazhagar reports and rejects. On that reading the verse meets 1076, where the base are like a beaten drum because they carry every மறை they hear to others; 1076 notes the harm to others, 847 the harm to the leaker.

Parimelazhagar reads 847 as a person who receives rare instruction and lets it run out without taking it in, harming himself. 418 says ears not pierced by listening are deaf even though they hear (கேட்பினுங் கேளாத் தகையவே). On that reading both describe teaching that reaches a person and does not enter; 847 adds that the loss is self-inflicted.

848 describes one who does not act when told and does not see for himself (ஏவவும் செய்கலான் தான் தேறான்), and calls that life a disease until it departs. 638 describes a king in the same two terms, one who destroys what the knowing say and does not know himself (அறிகொன்று அறியான்), and says the minister must still tell him what is sound. The same double failing appears in both; 848 gives the verdict on the person and 638 the duty of those beside him.

448 says a king without people who rebuke him will perish even with no one to ruin him (கெடுப்பாரிலானுங் கெடும்). 848 takes the case one step further: a person who has people to direct him and still does not act on it, and cannot work it out alone. 448 makes having correctors the safeguard; 848 shows the safeguard is useless to one who will not be corrected.

848 calls the life of one who neither heeds nor understands a disease until it leaves (போஒம் அளவுமோர் நோய்); Parimelazhagar takes this as a burden hard for the earth to bear, while Kalaignar takes the disease as the person's own. 572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a weight on the earth (உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை). On Parimelazhagar's reading the two share the figure of a person whose mere being alive is an affliction to the world.

849 says one who tries to show something to a person who does not see ends up the unseeing one, while that person goes on having seen it his own way (கண்டானாம் தான்கண்டவாறு). 929 says giving reasons to a drunk man is like searching with a flame for someone sunk under water (கீழ்நீர்க் குளித்தானைத் தீத்துரீஇ அற்று). Both describe instruction that cannot reach its target, and in both the effort reflects on the one making it.

849 ends with the unseeing person continuing to see as he saw (தான்கண்டவாறு). 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own underlying understanding prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்). Both hold that what is brought from outside, a teacher in 849 and books in 373, does not displace the understanding a person already has.

849 says the one who sets out to show something to a person who does not see becomes himself the unseeing one, which Parimelazhagar takes to mean that giving such a person good understanding is impossible. 638 says that even if the king destroys counsel and knows nothing himself, the one at his side is bound to say what is sound (உறுதி உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்). 638 limits 849: for a minister, the futility 849 describes does not cancel the duty to speak.

850 says one who says 'it is not' of what the world says is (உலகத்தார் உண்டென்பது இல்லென்பான்) will be set down as a demon on earth. 426 says understanding is to live with the world as the world lives (உலகத்தோடு அவ்வது உறைவது அறிவு). 426 gives the positive rule and 850 the penalty for breaking it, in the chapters on understanding and on its absence.

850 condemns the one who denies what the world affirms. 140 says those who have not learned to conduct themselves in accord with the world (உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்) lack understanding however much they have studied. Parimelazhagar takes 'the world' in both as the high-minded many, so both make their consensus a test that private cleverness does not override.

850 says the one who denies what the world says exists is counted a demon. 423 says understanding is to see the true substance of a thing whoever's mouth it is heard from (எப்பொருள் யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும் ... மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது). If உலகத்தார் means people at large, 850 makes agreement with them the standard, while 423 makes one's own discernment the standard whatever the source. The conflict eases on Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's reading of உலகத்தார் as the wise, whose settled view 423's examiner would also reach.
